meaning.evidence: The dialogue mostly survives verbatim, but words are wedged into stage directions and speaker tags ("Crikey, he gets up on a chair", "Anyway, HALE:", "Bugger me, MRS HALE:"), so who says what gets muddied. "Now, we left in such a hurry" and "ladies, mate?" add nothing true to the text.

sense.evidence: Several swaps miss the sense. "didn't get on properly well" for "very well". "Yeah, but nah, I don't mean anything" garbles the denial. "bugger all of a housekeeper" strains. "Crikey" in a stage direction makes no sense.

authenticity.evidence: Stage-Australian, with tags bolted on: "ladies, mate?", "loyal to your sex, I see, ay", "Blokes's mitts", "grotty bloody awful quick", and "Anyway," repeated as a filler.

register.evidence: Patchy: dense bolted-on slang in spots ("Sweet bugger-all", "mitts", "grotty bloody") over long untouched stretches ("I shouldn't say she had the homemaking instinct"). Swearing stays within dad level, but "Bugger me, MRS HALE" puts it in the wrong place.

tone.evidence: The quiet menace is undercut by comic tics: "Bugger me, MRS HALE: Yeah, but nah" and "would you say, ladies, mate?" turn tension into farce.

flow.evidence: Hard to read: "Anyway, HALE:", "Blokes's mitts", "grotty bloody awful quick" and "the blokes's steps on the stairs" break the grammar and the script format.

variety.evidence: The same few tics recur: "Anyway," four times, plus "mitts", "blokes's" and "bugger" more than once.

essence.evidence: The underlying scene is there, since it is mostly the original, but the garbling makes it hard to recognise as a play script: "Anyway, MRS HALE: (_stiffly_)".

problems.original: HALE: Well, women are used to worrying over trifles.
problems.why: A filler is inserted in front of the speaker tag, which breaks the script format. This recurs throughout ("Anyway, MRS HALE:", "Bugger me, MRS HALE:").

problems.quote: Crikey, he gets up on a chair
problems.original: He gets up on a chair
problems.why: An exclamation inside a stage direction makes no sense.
"Mate" addressed to the women is wrong and comic, and it is stacked after "ladies".
A pile-up of intensifiers, and swearing out of character for Mrs Hale's stiff reply.

A.summary: A mechanical, broken pass. Tags and swears are spliced into stage directions and speaker names, and it wrecks both the format and the tension.

meaning.evidence: Nearly everything is kept. "frettin' over little things" drops the pointed word "trifles". "Whatever Mrs Peters takes'll be right, surely" and Mrs Peters' "Well, it's only their job, I s'pose" soften her conviction slightly. "like a young pollie after a vote" is light colour.

sense.evidence: Mostly exact: "has another squiz", "stickybeaking about", "picking holes in everything", "jam jars", "Not much... Bugger all of a housekeeper". "Bugger all of a housekeeper" strains a little as phrasing, and "don't thaw an inch" mixes two idioms.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like real Australian speech: "Sweet bugger-all here but kitchen stuff", "Yeah, nah, I don't mean anything", "Seems a bit rough, bagging her". "where would we be without the ladies, ay?" is fine.

register.evidence: A solid level 4 that keeps it a play rather than a pub yarn. The swearing ("bugger-all", "Bugger all") is within dad level.

tone.evidence: The tension and the condescension survive: "Filthy towels!" and "I'd hate to have men traipsin' into my kitchen, stickybeaking about". "Sweet bugger-all" gives the Sheriff a slightly jokier edge.

flow.evidence: Reads naturally aloud throughout: "Haven't set foot in this house in more than a year."

variety.evidence: Good spread: squiz, mitts, beaut, grotty, stickybeaking, picking holes, spick and span, keep your eyes peeled.

essence.evidence: Clearly Glaspell's scene, with the gender undercurrent intact, but losing "trifles", the play's title word and its point, is a real cost.

problems.quote: women are used to frettin' over little things
problems.original: women are used to worrying over trifles
problems.why: "Trifles" is the play's title and its thematic hinge. Swapping it for "little things" loses that.

problems.quote: Well, it's only their job, I s'pose.
problems.original: Of course it's no more than their duty.
problems.why: "I s'pose" softens Mrs Peters' dutiful certainty.

problems.quote: the women don't thaw an inch
problems.why: A mixed idiom ("thaw" and "give an inch").
"Bugger all of a" is a strained construction.

B.summary: A natural, well-pitched level-4 retelling. Its main loss is the key word "trifles".

meaning.evidence: Every beat survives, including "trifles". "might've put a bit of this muck on it himself" only spells out Mrs Hale's implication. "sticking up for the sisterhood" is a fair rendering of "loyal to your sex".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "Not much chop as a housekeeper", "a fair whack of work", "the lie of the land", "carryin' on about her jam". "here's a bloody mess" drops the irony of "nice mess" slightly.

authenticity.evidence: Natural and local: "wouldn't it rot your socks", "Not much chop", "has a look on a shelf", "hops up on a chair". "Well, wouldn't it rot your socks, women!" is slightly awkward with "women" tacked on.

register.evidence: Level 4 in voice and slang, kept to a light dad-level "bloody". If anything a shade lighter than B, but on brief.

tone.evidence: The tension and the men's condescension come through: "Locked up for murder and she's carryin' on about her jam." The women's quiet solidarity stays.

flow.evidence: Smooth throughout: "Seems a bit rough, bagging her for not having the place spick and span when she had to clear out in such a hurry."

variety.evidence: Varied (squiz, chop, fair whack, rot your socks, yarn, traipsing), but "bagging" appears twice in the closing lines and "clear out" or "cleared out" twice.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably Trifles, with the title word, the dashes and the undercurrent all retained.

problems.why: "Nice mess" is dry irony. "Bloody mess" is literal.

problems.quote: Well, wouldn't it rot your socks, women!
problems.original: Well, can you beat the women!
problems.why: The idiom is good, but ", women!" sits awkwardly after it.

problems.quote: sticking their noses in and bagging everything
problems.why: "Bagging" recurs a few lines later ("bagging her").

C.summary: The strongest: faithful, natural, and keeps "trifles" and the scene's tension, with only small repetition.
